Neonatal common thresher sharks emerge at a fork length of approximately 81 cm [Lb = approximately 81 cm], a size that reflects substantial in utero yolk dependence. During the immediate post-partum period, while the yolk sac is completely resorbed at total lengths between 12 and 40 cm, the pups transition rapidly to exogenous feeding, targeting small pelagic prey. Field data suggest that in the warm, productive waters of the California Current, maintained at a mean temperature of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C], the gestation period yields a calculated age at birth of about 620 days [ab = about 620 days]. This protracted embryonic development is typical of lamniform sharks and is associated with the production of relatively advanced, well-provisioned neonates that face minimal predation pressure from other pelagic piscivores immediately upon entry into the pelagic environment.

The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size, with females achieving a considerably larger asymptotic fork length than males. The ultimate fork length for females reaches 274.5 cm [Li = 274.5 cm], a dimension that enables them to pursue larger prey items and likely confers a fecundity advantage. Males, by contrast, attain a more modest ultimate fork length of 228 cm [Li = 228 cm], a disparity that becomes apparent during the sub-adult growth phase. This difference in maximum size is reflected in the corresponding ultimate wet weights; females achieve an estimated asymptotic body mass of 293,800 grams [Wwi = 293,800 grams], while males reach only 174,200 grams [Wwi = 174,200 grams]. Such pronounced dimorphism is a common feature among pelagic sharks and is thought to be driven by differential energetic allocation, with females investing heavily in somatic growth to support large litters.

Females of the common thresher enter reproductive maturity at a fork length of roughly 216 cm [Lp = roughly 216 cm], a size that is corroborated by vertebral analyses. At this size, the estimated wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 149,600 grams [Wwp = approximately 149,600 grams]. Males, by contrast, attain puberty at a smaller fork length of 188 cm [Lp = 188 cm], and their estimated wet weight at puberty for males is about 101,200 grams [Wwp = about 101,200 grams]. This earlier maturation in males is a widespread pattern among elasmobranchs and likely reflects the selective advantage of reaching a size sufficient for successful clasper-mediated fertilisation before females, who must allocate more energy to gestational costs.

Reproductive output in the common thresher is constrained by a relatively low fecundity, with each gravid female producing between two and four pups per litter [N_R_i = between two and four pups per litter] in a single annual reproductive event [F_R_i = single annual reproductive event]. This modest litter size is consistent with the species' life history strategy as a slow-growing, late-maturing pelagic predator. Under the thermal regime of the California Current, where surface waters average 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females has been estimated at approximately 12 years [tp = approximately 12 years], while males achieve sexual maturity more rapidly, reaching puberty around 8 years after birth [tp = around 8 years after birth]. This sex-specific difference in maturation time aligns with the observed dimorphism in size at puberty and the earlier reproductive activation of males.

The maximum lifespan of the common thresher is considerable for a pelagic shark, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of about 25 years [am = about 25 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 23.2 °C [T = 23.2 °C]. This longevity is consistent with a life history in which reproductive senescence is delayed and iteroparity is the norm. The species' slow growth rate and extended generation time render it particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as population recovery from depletion requires multiple decades. Comparative analyses within the family Alopiidae suggest that the common thresher's lifespan is intermediate, falling between the shorter-lived pelagic thresher and the longer-lived bigeye thresher, a pattern that may reflect differences in habitat depth and metabolic demand.
